doc.title: Hubert Laws — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Mongo Santamaria and early recording sessions
title: Laws's own 1968 Atlantic session with harpsichord and bassoon
summary: Brown asks about the 1968 session with Roland Hanna on harpsichord, Carl Porter on bassoon and Melba Moore. Laws agrees his early records were made for commercial reasons.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: The next one is under your name, a session, 1968. This is the one that has Sir Roland Hanna playing harpsichord. You’re playing flute, piccolo. I guess maybe there are some other dates, but it seems like, at this point, more focus on the flute, less doubling. Carl Porter, bassoon, Chuck Rainey, electric bass, Grady Tate, drums. This is Atlantic. And then probably a corollary session, different personnel, Jimmy Owens, still Carl Porter on bassoon. So I thought maybe we could talk about that. Kenny Burrell on guitar.
The fact that you’re bringing in a bassoon – I presume that’s your idea, but Carl Porter . . .
This is 1968. It’s Atlantic. It’s got Melba Moore singing on a song, No More.

Yeah, I wrote that. I remember that. I remember bringing her in to sing that lyric. That No More has two sets of lyrics. Jon Hendricks wrote a set for it. He’s in the habit of doing stuff like that. I saw him at the NEA, too. He’s in the habit of doing that, but he wrote a set of lyrics which ended up being done by Lou Rawls, No More. But no, I don’t recall that session, other than the fact, I think I wrote something called I Wish You Knew or something like that.
Yeah, and I remember bringing the bassoon in on that.
Yeah. It says sitar, too. Sam Brolsh played sitar?

No. Sam’s last name’s something else. I don’t know where they got that Brolsh from. He died, too. I remember Sam. He used to do a lot of sessions. But Sam had another last name, like Wagner or something.
What caught my eye was Sir Roland Hanna – whom I had the pleasure of playing with – harpsichord. I never heard him play harpsichord. That’s what got me on this one.
I do remember somewhat that session. But I don’t like that music. You hear it. It’s weird.

Let me quote you on the liner notes. This is what Dan Morgenstern said – penned these. He says, “And he began to make records of his own, the first few” – and then he’s quoting you, “Not really representative of the direction in which I wanted to go. They were made for commercial reasons.”
So I think you corroborated that quote. So there’s no doubt there.
